## PART 13: META ANDROMEDA COMPLIANCE (SMO Framework)

> Source: Meta Andromeda Blueprint (Evan Seech, Sell More Online)

This section details the specific creative diversity requirements from Meta's Andromeda retrieval engine update, supplementing the Andromeda overview already in Part 5 of this skill.

### 13.1 What Andromeda Actually Does

Andromeda is a change in the **ad retrieval process** (the first step in how Meta serves ads). It sifts through millions of possible ad candidates and narrows them to a few thousand most relevant ads, which then pass to the ranking stage (Lattice).

**Key facts:**
- Andromeda can now sift through **10,000x more ads** at any given time
- Your 3-5 new creatives per week are competing against an OCEAN of content
- "The system uses complex latent relationships between people's interests, products, and services to deliver more personalized ads" (Meta)
- Andromeda has already led to an 8% improvement in ads quality (Meta's measurement)
- Fully rolled out by ~October 2025 across all accounts

### 13.2 The 3 Dimensions of Creative Diversity

Meta's definition of creative diversification requires variation across three specific dimensions:

| Dimension | Definition | What "Same" Looks Like (PENALIZED) | What "Different" Looks Like (REWARDED) |
|-----------|-----------|------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| **Theme** | Topic/ad angle -- the subject of the ad | All ads about "scaling ads" | Ad 1: pricing ceiling, Ad 2: referral dependency, Ad 3: price shopping, Ad 4: creative fatigue |
| **Messaging** | What you actually say -- the specific words | "The #1 way to fix show rates is X" vs. "The best way to fix show rates is X" (NOT varied) | Completely different pain points, desires, case studies, circumstances articulated per ad |
| **Visuals** | Editing + Environment + Creator in the video | Same creator + same setting = same ad to Meta | Different camera angles, locations, shirts, creators, editing styles, aspect ratios |

**All three must vary together.** Changing one dimension while keeping the other two the same will still be penalized.

### 13.3 The Creative Similarity Penalty

Meta is rolling out a **Creative Similarity metric** that shows how similar your ads are to each other. You will be penalized if they are too similar.

**How Meta determines similarity:**
- Two ads are "identical" if they share similar messaging, visuals, and especially the **first 3 seconds**
- Even if copy, message, or CTA is different, similar visuals = same ad
- Slight copy changes will NOT be recognized as a "new ad" or "new concept"

**Specific similarity triggers:**
- Same creator + same setting = same ad
- Same messaging + same visuals = same ad
- Hook & Body method with little variation = same thing to same people

**Consequence:** Meta will only serve one of the "duplicate" ads, effectively wasting your creative slots and limiting your reach.

### 13.4 Persona-Based Ad Creation Exercise

Instead of creating "one-size-fits-all" ads, create ads built around specific sub-avatars (personas):

**Step 1: Define 1-4 avatars you sell to**
Example for a paid ads agency:
- Avatar 1: Coaches spending < $500/day on ads (confused about scaling)
- Avatar 2: Coaches spending > $500/day on ads (need expert help)
- Avatar 3: Coaches NOT running ads (afraid to start)

**Step 2: List all reasons/pains/desires/circumstances per avatar**
Example for Avatar 1 (coaches < $500/day):
- Confused about how to scale
- Hired agencies before that didn't work
- Keep turning ads off and on with no consistency
- Struggling to work the ads manager
- Threw together a funnel with freelancers and it has holes
- Cannot figure out why ads won't scale
- Copying competitors and still not working

**Step 3: Each reason becomes its own INDIVIDUAL ad**
- Hook centered on ONE specific reason/pain/desire/circumstance
- Body supports that specific hook (can "pepper in" 1-2 related angles)
- CTA aligned to the central theme
- Film as one cohesive unit from start to finish

**Protein powder example (41 angles for one product):**
1. Organic ingredients, 2. Clean ingredients, 3. Doesn't clump, 4. High absorption, 5. Celebrity endorsement, 6. Tastes good, 7. Available locally, 8. Budget-friendly, 9. Stays full longer, 10. Kills cravings, 11. Has collagen, 12. Low calorie, 13. Tired of bars, 14. Tired of cooking, 15. Fits busy routine, 16. Has creatine, 17. Beef organs, 18. Not lab-made, 19. Third-party tested, 20. Low sugar, 21. Great with water, 22. Great with milk, 23. Meal replacement, 24. US-made/2-day shipping, 25. No fillers/gums, 26. No seed oils, 27. No artificial flavors, 28. Third-party clean, 29. Nutrient dense, 30. Blends into smoothies, 31. Supports energy, 32. No midday crash, 33. Overall wellness, 34. For hardcore athletes, 35. For casual fitness, 36. For leisure athletes, 37. No Yellow 5/Blue 5/Red 40, 38. Baking recipes, 39. Added colostrum, 40. No bloating, 41. No microplastics

Each is its OWN ad reaching a DIFFERENT type of person through Andromeda.

### 13.5 The Two Paths to Andromeda Success

| Path | Volume | Diversity | Creative Lifespan | Best For |
|------|--------|-----------|-------------------|----------|
| **Path 1: High Volume** | 50+ creatives per week | Can be narrower in messaging range | Shorter (fatigue quicker, relaunch weekly) | Large teams, agencies with production capacity (~200 creatives/month) |
| **Path 2: Diverse Messaging** | 15-20+ unique ads per month (minimum 30 individualized ads per launch) | Wide range of themes, each ad a different reason to buy | Longer lifespan per ad | Most businesses. Accounts implementing this saw ZERO cost inflation during rollout. |

### 13.6 Hook & Body Method: Updated Guidance

**Old practice (pre-Andromeda):** Film 10-30 hooks and 1-2 bodies, splice them. Majority of each video export is the same.

**Current reality:** Hook & Body method only works now if you launch 50+ new creatives per week. They fatigue quicker. For most businesses, this is unsustainable.

**New best practice:** Film full-length individualized ads from start to finish. Hook, Body, CTA all aligned around one specific reason. This gives better longevity.

**"Sprinkling In" technique:** The hook should be centered around ONE central pain/desire/outcome. You CAN pepper in other angles in the body, but they should support and flow from the central hook. (See the annotated MSP ad scripts in the Andromeda Blueprint source for detailed examples.)

### 13.7 Creative Iteration Under Andromeda

When you find a winning theme, you can "play within that sandbox" -- but differently than before:

**What NO LONGER works:**
- Reshoot with same words in different shirt
- Duplicate campaign with 90% same creatives and minor tweaks

**What DOES work when iterating a winner:**
- Fully rescripted ad in a different setting (change the visual AND the words)
- New diverse individualized ads WITHIN that theme (same theme, different messaging)
- Different editing style, especially in first 3 seconds
- Weave in new B-roll
- Change the creator/actor
- Try new ad format (educational, testimonial, case study, demo, selfie, skit)
- If winning ad was outcome-driven, try desire-driven, pain-driven, or curiosity-driven hooks on same theme

**Visual variation checklist for iterations:**
- New locations (inside/outside/different background)
- New creator in the ad
- New camera angles
- Different shirts (film 3-5 in one outfit, switch for next 3-5)
- Weave in current events or "grand narrative"
- New ad format (carousel, static, etc.)
- Recycle winners with fresh B-roll
- Change aspect ratios (4:5, 9:16, 4:5 with banner, 1:1)

**Key rule:** ALWAYS continue feeding the algorithm with DIFFERENT and NEW themes, even while doubling down on winning themes.

### 13.8 Influencing Lattice (The Ranking Stage)

After Andromeda (retrieval), ads pass to Lattice (ranking) which pairs ads with users most probable to convert using the Total Value Equation:

```
Total Value = Advertiser Bid + Estimated Action Rate + Ad Quality
```

**Ad Quality is comprised of:**
- Quality Ranking (Below Average / Average / Above Average)
- Engagement Rate Ranking
- Conversion Rate Ranking

**How to influence Lattice:**
1. **Messaging in your ad** -- hyper-contextual ads speaking to real-time needs
2. **Pixel conditioning** -- only clean, qualified data reported back
3. **Visuals of your ad** -- native-looking, high-quality, engaging

**Key insight:** Even with a SMALLER budget, if your ads are hyper-contextual you can get priority placements and great results (high Estimated Action Rate compensates for lower bid).

### 13.9 Reaching New Audiences Under Andromeda

Three levers to widen reach:

| Lever | How It Works |
|-------|-------------|
| **Change standard event optimization** | Different events reach different user pools. People who convert on "Schedule" are different from "Submit Application." Each user's conversion history determines which ads they see. |
| **Widen messaging** | Feed Andromeda more diverse creatives and angles. New ad angles referring to audience with different names (e.g., "Ecom Brands" vs. "DTC Brands"). New visuals. |
| **Swap ad format** | Video watchers get served videos. Image engagers get served images. IG Shop users get shop-optimized ads. Exploit behavioral differences. |

**Formula for Meta success:** Messaging + Pixel Conditioning + Ad Quality + Diversification + Campaign Objective = KEY components

### 13.10 Writing Ads with LLMs (Andromeda-Compliant)

When using an LLM for ad scripting:
- Always check and edit outputs manually
- Remove "marketing-y" language and make it sound human
- Add more directness
- CTAs from LLMs are typically rough -- train it with feedback and examples
- Feed in call transcripts (10-15+ qualified calls from varying types of people) for diverse angle discovery
- Use the persona-based exercise to prompt the LLM for diverse ad angles per avatar
- Run scripts through hemingwayapp.com -- adjust to 5th grade reading level or below

## PART 14: CONTRADICTION RESOLUTION -- DYNAMIC CREATIVE

### The Conflict

**Existing skill position (Part 1, Section 1.2 -- "Trust the Algorithm"):** Use Dynamic Creative. Supply 10 videos, 5 headlines, 5 body copy texts = 250 combinations. Let the platform test automatically.

**SMO position (Launching Meta Ads Blueprint + Andromeda Blueprint):** "We are NOT using Dynamic Creative. We launch Individual Ads." 20-30 individual ads per ad set, each with the same 3-5 body copy, 3-5 headlines, and 1-2 descriptions attached.

### Why SMO Moved Away from Dynamic Creative

1. **Andromeda changed the game.** Dynamic Creative lets the platform mix-and-match elements, but Andromeda now evaluates the first 3 seconds and overall creative similarity. Spliced combinations may register as "same ad" to the algorithm.
2. **Control.** Individual ads give the media buyer full visibility into which exact creative is performing, making it easier to iterate on winners and kill losers.
3. **Full-length individualized ads last longer.** Under Andromeda, ads where Hook + Body + CTA are aligned around one cohesive theme have better longevity than spliced combinations.
4. **Creative similarity penalty.** Dynamic Creative variations that share the same body/CTA may be flagged as similar, reducing their effective reach.

### When Each Approach Can Work

| Approach | Best For | Tradeoffs |
|----------|----------|-----------|
| **Dynamic Creative (existing skill)** | Quick testing of messaging variations when production capacity is limited. Good for finding winning elements (which headline resonates? which body copy?). Lower barrier to entry. | Less control over exact combinations served. May hit creative similarity penalty faster. Hook-swapping lasts shorter duration. |
| **Individual Ads (SMO)** | Maximum control and Andromeda compliance. Full visibility into per-ad performance. Better for scaling. Each ad is a cohesive unit filmed start-to-finish. | Requires more production effort (20-30 unique ads per ad set). Needs robust scripting pipeline. More creative capacity required. |

### Recommendation

**For new clients or testing phases:** Either approach can work. Dynamic Creative is faster to set up for initial signal gathering.

**For scaling and Andromeda optimization:** Transition to Individual Ads following the SMO campaign structure. Film full-length individualized ads with cohesive Hook-Body-CTA alignment. This is the approach showing the best longevity and stability at scale as of late 2025.

**Let the user decide** based on their production capacity and current phase. Present both options and their tradeoffs.

## APPENDIX: Ad Creative Iteration at Scale (Merged from ad-creative skill)

> Unique frameworks for performance-based creative iteration and batch generation. Complements the strategy above with structured testing workflows.

### Platform Character Specs (Quick Reference)

| Platform | Headline | Description | Primary Text |
|----------|----------|-------------|-------------|
| **Google RSA** | 30 chars (up to 15) | 90 chars (up to 4) | N/A |
| **Meta** | 40 chars rec | 30 chars rec | 125 visible (2,200 max) |
| **LinkedIn** | 70 chars rec (200 max) | 100 chars rec (300 max) | 150 rec (600 max) |
| **TikTok** | N/A | N/A | 80 chars rec (100 max) |
| **Twitter/X** | 70 chars (card) | 200 chars (card) | 280 chars (tweet) |

### Angle Category Matrix

Before writing variations, establish 3-5 distinct angles:

| Category | Example |
|----------|---------|
| Pain point | "Stop wasting time on X" |
| Outcome | "Achieve Y in Z days" |
| Social proof | "Join 10,000+ teams who..." |
| Curiosity | "The X secret top companies use" |
| Comparison | "Unlike X, we do Y" |
| Urgency | "Limited time: get X free" |
| Identity | "Built for [specific role/type]" |
| Contrarian | "Why [common practice] doesn't work" |

### Wave-Based Batch Generation

For large-scale creative production (100+ variations per cycle):

**Wave 1: Core angles** — 3-5 angles, 5 variations each = 15-25 pieces
**Wave 2: Extended variations** — Double down on top 2 performing angles
**Wave 3: Wild cards** — Contrarian, emotional, hyper-specific angles

Quality filter after each wave: remove over-limit, deduplicate, flag policy violations, verify headline/description combos make sense together.

### Performance Iteration Loop

When user provides performance data (CSV, paste, or dashboard):

**Step 1: Analyze Winners** — By CTR, conversion rate, or ROAS:
- Winning themes (what pain points appear in top performers?)
- Winning structures (questions? statements? numbers?)
- Winning word patterns (specific recurring phrases?)
- Character utilization (are top performers shorter or longer?)

**Step 2: Analyze Losers** — What angles fall flat, what patterns appear in low performers

**Step 3: Generate New Variations** — Double down on winners with fresh phrasing, extend winning angles into new variations, test 1-2 new unexplored angles, avoid loser patterns

**Step 4: Document the Iteration**
```
## Iteration Log
- Round: [number]
- Top performers: [list with metrics]
- Winning patterns: [summary]
- New variations: [count] headlines, [count] descriptions
- New angles being tested: [list]
- Angles retired: [list]
```

### Bulk CSV Output Format

For direct platform upload:
```csv
headline_1,headline_2,headline_3,description_1,description_2,platform
"Stop Manual Reporting","Automate in 5 Minutes","Join 10K+ Teams","Save 10+ hrs/week. Start free.","Connect once. Reports forever.","google_ads"
```

### Common Creative Mistakes

- Writing RSA headlines that only work together (they get combined randomly)
- Ignoring character limits (platforms truncate without warning)
- All variations sound the same (vary angles, not just word choice)
- No CTA headlines (always include action-oriented options)
- Iterating without data (gut feelings < metrics)
- Testing too many variables at once (one change per test cycle)
- Retiring creative too early (allow 1,000+ impressions before judging)

## Core Job

Write email sequences that convert booked leads into closed deals, manage ongoing list engagement, and maximize every email touchpoint in the funnel:
- **Pre-call** (72 hours before the call): Build trust, handle objections, set expectations, maximize show rate
- **Post-call** (7-14 days after no-close): Re-engage, overcome final objections, create urgency
- **No-show** (5-7 days): Re-book leads who didn't show up
- **Opt-in sequences** (5 emails over 5 days): Convert VSL/lead magnet opt-ins who didn't immediately book
- **Broadcast emails** (ongoing weekly): Maintain list engagement using 4 strategic cadence models
- **Breakout video scripts** (thank-you page): 10 micro-videos that prevent no-shows
- **Campaign flows** (ongoing): Launch sequences, re-engagement, post-purchase onboarding

> **Routing Note:** This skill handles **high-ticket booked-call funnel emails** — pre-call nurture, post-call follow-up, no-show recovery, broadcast strategies, and the Email Matrix segmentation methodology. Use when the funnel ends in a **sales call** (VSL → book call, webinar → book call, D100 → book call). If the funnel ends in a **checkout or opt-in** and you need welcome, nurture, conversion, launch, or re-engagement sequences (no sales call), use **email-sequences** instead.

# PART 1: THE EMAIL MATRIX — CORE PHILOSOPHY

## Context = More Money

This is the foundational principle of the entire Email Matrix methodology. Most organizations send robotic, generalized, sterile emails to their entire list and are shocked when they get low open rates and overall low email engagement.

**The fix:** Create context as much as you possibly can based on the data you have available in your CRM and from the segmentation you can create.

**The investment company example:** A client markets to investors who want the company to manage millions of dollars for them. Each investor that applies must answer with the amount they want to invest ($1M or less, $1M-$5M, $5M-$10M, $10M-$20M, $20M-$50M, $50M+). The difference between a lead that says they have $1M to invest and an investor with $50M+ is WIDE. They need to be treated differently — the strategies deployed to manage their money are different, so the communication must be crafted contextually for that person and their needs. If the person with $50M gets treated the same and you go over strategies of turning $1M into 12% a year more, it turns them off and you substantially lower your probability of converting.

**The solution:** Create a video series emailed out in a sequence to each type of lead for strategies that would be deployed to best manage their desired investable range. The concerns of these different ranges differ greatly too — address those in subsequent emails so each person knows their situation is known by the company, which makes people feel great.

**The Fear of God example:** Jeremy spent thousands on clothes from Fear of God — only ever bought black men's clothes in XXL, lives in Miami Florida. What he never gets (but would catch his attention 1000X more): an email that says "our latest black mens clothes in XXL" or "the perfect outfit for Miami summertime." The data exists in their CRM. The contextual communication would exponentially increase purchase frequency.

**The bank analogy:** Ever been on a call with a bank, had to get transferred, and had to repeat your entire story to the next rep? How frustrating is that? How good does it feel when the first rep explains everything to the new one before the handoff? Night and day difference. It's the same with your leads — when you tailor communication specific to their needs, wants, and desires using all the data you've collected, you increase spending probability by a lot.

**Core rule:** From here forward, ask at least one segmentation question in every lead form you've got, even if it's something simple like a newsletter opt-in. Get something — anything — that allows you to communicate in a more specific way rather than just throwing them into that generalized email list.

It's about slicing your list into smaller, more manageable groups based on certain traits they share. Think of it as the difference between a shotgun and a sniper rifle. The shotgun scatters, hoping to hit anything in its path, but the sniper rifle aims, targets, and hits with incredible accuracy. Your email marketing should be that sniper rifle.

---

## Complete 14-Way Email Segmentation System

The sharper your segments, the more your emails will feel like they're speaking directly to each recipient. Tags are unique identifiers you attach to customer data in your CRM system. They allow you to group people based on their needs and interests so that when it's time for marketing, they get the right message at the right time.

### Segment 1: Demographic Slice (Who They Are)
Think age, income, job. Why chat about retirement plans with a college kid? Tailor your message to fit their life stage.

### Segment 2: Geographic Segment (Where They're At)
Location, location, location. It's not just for real estate. From local events to weather shifts, make your emails resonate with local flavor.

### Segment 3: Behavioral Breakdown (What They Do)
Look at their shopping behavior, website clicks, and past interactions. Like a detective, use clues from their actions to personalize your approach.

### Segment 4: Engagement Filter (How They Interact)
Some folks devour your emails; others glance. Segment by engagement to keep the avid readers fueled and try to rekindle the spark with the skimmers.

### Segment 5: Buying Behavior (Past Purchases)
Like a chef suggesting wine based on your meal, recommend products related to their past purchases. It's about enhancing their experience.

### Segment 6: Sales Funnel Focus (Journey Stage)
Tailor your content like you're guiding them down a path. Newbies get the 101 content, while veterans might see the finish line offers.

### Segment 7: VIP Section (Loyalty Level)
Roll out the red carpet for your regulars with exclusive deals or sneak peeks. Show them love, and they'll keep coming back.

### Segment 8: Abandoned Cart Crew (Almost Buyers)
For those who left their cart lonely, a gentle nudge or a tempting offer might just get them across the finish line.

### Segment 9: Email Cadence Club (Their Pace)
Some like it hot, some like it not. Adjust your send rate to match their preference, keeping them cozy and connected without the overwhelm.

### Segment 10: Lead Magnet Group (Interest Indicator)
Segment by the freebies they've snagged. It's a window into their interests and how you can serve them next.

### Segment 11: Survey Squad (Opinion Owners)
Use survey insights to tailor your messages, addressing their specific feedback or interests with precision.

### Segment 12: Membership/Subscription Status
Different strokes for different folks. Customize your content based on the level of access or service they've signed up for.

### Segment 13: Seasonal Shoppers
Some customers come alive during certain seasons. Identify these patterns and you can be there with the right offer at the right time.

### Segment 14: Event Enthusiasts
For those who've shown up to your events, keep the conversation going. Offer resources, or tease the next big thing.

### Bonus: Tech Tendencies
Knowing if they're team mobile or desktop can help you design emails that hit the mark, visually and contextually.

## Email Send Time & Day Optimization Rules

Data compiled from millions of emails sent over a 365-day period across many different niches.

### Best Time of Day
- **Best:** 3 PM in the person's timezone (not your timezone, THEIR timezone)
- **Best range:** Noon to 6 PM
- **Worst times:** Anytime after 9 PM through 11 AM the following day
- **Exception:** Order notifications and support response emails perform best in the morning
- **Rule:** Content and value-driven emails that are lengthier or intended to get the person to browse for several minutes perform best in late afternoon

### Best Days of the Week
- **Best days:** Tuesday and Friday (beat the next highest days by a full 9% additional open rate on average)
- **Worst days:** Saturday and Sunday
- **Middle tier:** Monday and Wednesday (decent), Thursday (lags behind slightly)

### Day-of-Week Strategy
- **Tuesday and Friday:** Send sales-based emails that could lead to revenue — more trackable revenue compared to any other days
- **Weekends:** Send content emails instead — drive email traffic to social media channels or educational funnels/lead magnets that have a lot of consumption time since people generally have more time on weekends
- **Business-specific:** Most businesses have one part of the week that's great and one part that's slower. Be aware of that trend and play into it.

---

## Why People Open Emails — Complete Survey Data

Survey data from email lists of clients, compiled into ranked order:

### Rank 1: "Expecting It" (DOMINANT reason)
They opted into something expecting an access email. They contacted customer support and are expecting a response. They replied to an email and are expecting a response back. This was the most dominant reason by far.

**Tactical implication:** Think "how can I get all of my emails to be expected." That happens after someone knowingly opts in and is actively waiting for what you're going to send.

**"Email Options" technique:** Give leads the ability to select different options for what they want to see next (represented by buttons or links): content, top videos of the week, newsletter content, offers/sales/discounts, more of the same, and whatever else is applicable. This also helps with further segmentation.

### Rank 2: Known Sender
Known senders have a higher likelihood of being opened. When you shop with companies you love, you open any email they send because you love that company. Same for brands you support or newsletters you're opted into and want to read. Unknown senders = brands they haven't heard from before.

### Rank 3: Subject Line
Third place behind expectations and sender recognition.

### Rank 4: Preview Text
Well behind in fourth place.

### Rank 5: Offer
Last place — the actual offer itself.

---

## Email Value Provision Types

In an era where inboxes are inundated with "buy now" and "limited time offer" emails, standing out requires delivering real, tangible value — not just relentless sales pitches.

### Type 1: Educational Content
Share insights, tutorials, and how-tos that align with your audience's interests and needs. If you're a financial services company and you know a segment is new homeowners, send a guide on managing home-related expenses.

### Type 2: Personalized Recommendations
Use data to offer personalized product suggestions, articles, or services. If someone's been browsing winter coats, send a curated selection of coats with care tips for winter apparel.

### Type 3: Exclusive Content
Content exclusive to email subscribers: early access to sales, sneak peeks at new products, or content created specifically for the list like an in-depth industry report.

### Type 4: Interactive Elements
Polls, surveys, or quizzes that engage and provide insights into subscriber preferences. This makes subscribers feel heard and offers more aligned content.

### Type 5: Behind-the-Scenes Looks
Stories about how products are made, team introductions, virtual tours of office or manufacturing. Humanizes your brand and builds deeper connection.

### The Golden Thread: Context
The more you know about subscribers (purchase history, engagement, willingly shared info) the more tailored and impactful your value-driven emails can be. Context transforms generic advice into "This was written for me" moments.

## ESP Requirements (What Email Service Providers Want)

Understanding ESPs is critical — they determine whether your emails reach the inbox or languish in spam.

### 1. Deliverability Is King
ESPs scrutinize sender reputation, engagement rates, and content quality. Your mission: prove your emails are not just wanted but welcomed.

### 2. Quality Over Quantity
ESPs prioritize senders who provide high-value content over those who bombard with high volume of low-quality. Mantra: send less, but send better.

### 3. Engagement Drives Favor
Open rates, click-through rates, and interaction frequency are all scrutinized. High engagement = boosted sender reputation and inbox placement.

### 4. Authenticity and Transparency
Clear "from" information, straightforward subject lines, easy-to-find unsubscribe options. Misleading practices are penalized.

### 5. Consistency Is Key
Consistent sending frequency and volume helps ESPs trust your patterns. Erratic sending triggers spam alarms.

### 6. List Hygiene Practices
Regularly remove unengaged subscribers, correct misspelled addresses, manage bounce rates. Signals you're a conscientious sender.

### 7. Adherence to Regulations
Compliance with CAN-SPAM, GDPR, etc. Direct reflection of commitment to ethical email practices.

### 8. Feedback Loop Utilization
Use ESP feedback loops (notification when recipients mark emails as spam) to adjust strategy and maintain positive relationships.

## Subject Line Optimization Rules

### Optimal Word Count
- **Best:** 6-10 words (12% higher open rate vs. 0-5 or 11-15 words)
- **Severe dropoff:** Above 15 words
- **Mobile reality:** Typical iPhone screen cuts off around 10 one-to-two syllable words
- **Desktop exception:** Older demographics viewing on desktop may benefit from longer subject lines

### Formatting Rules
- **Punctuation:** Limit to three punctuation marks max per subject line. Overdoing it sends emails to spam.
- **Preferred style:** No punctuation, lowercase sentencing = max open rates
- **Emojis:** Use sparingly — max one emoji to complement, not overshadow. They display differently across devices. Preview before sending.
- **Personalization:** Use "Personal Touch Tags" (recipient's name, location) to boost open rates. Especially effective with targeted outreach, customer milestones, or post-purchase.
- **Directness:** Be direct and concise. Avoid seasonal cliches ("Falling into discounts"). Highlight tangible benefits instead.
- **Character limit:** No more than 60 characters for maximum mobile digestibility.

### Testing Protocol
- A/B test subject lines by sending variants to different segments
- Keep a running doc of what's worked and what hasn't
- Review open rates of recent subject lines to illuminate what captures attention
- Most CRMs have built-in A/B testing functions

## "Keep It Simple and Remind Them" Email Template

When you run paid ads to a sales team used to organic leads, they'll say leads "didn't know who we are." This email fixes that immediately.

### What It Is
Take a screenshot of the ad(s) they responded to, the sales page or lead form they filled out, and send them their application data that they answered with, along with any links for wherever they originated from as a lead.

### When to Use
- Works best for leads that are then going to speak with a sales team
- NOT needed for ecommerce brands or lead magnets where there is no sales team verbal communication
- Send as soon as the lead comes in OR before the scheduled call

### Why It Works
It's amazing that leads forget after minutes or a few hours that they took the time to go through your lead funnel, but it happens. Reminding them of where they originated from increases show rates and establishes familiarity bias which leads to higher trust right away.

### Template Structure
1. Screenshot of the ad they responded to
2. Screenshot of the sales page/lead form
3. Their application data (answers they submitted)
4. Links to where they came from
5. Load it up with Credibility Assets (see below)

---

## Credibility Assets System (Complete)

If you didn't need to send where the lead originated from, start off your sequence with credibility assets. These drastically increase the odds of a lead buying from your sales team in a shorter sales cycle.

### Asset Types
1. **Third-party verified testimonial sites** (TrustPilot, etc.)
2. **Company website URLs**
3. **Company addresses for physical locations**
4. **Phone numbers**
5. **Team photos**
6. **Links to social channels**
7. **Anything that makes the lead conclude:** "this company is legit, I'm excited to buy from them"

### For E-Commerce Companies
Add:
- **Unboxing videos**
- **Instructional "how to use" videos**
- **"What to expect" videos**
- **Third-party YouTube reviews** (great for lowering buyer's remorse post-purchase)
- **Thank-you videos from staff** (leverages law of specificity — e.g., "4.7 stars out of 5" is more believable than "5/5")

### Contextual Cross-Sell Example (Fully/Herman Miller)
- Buyer of standing desk gets "how to put it together" video, then "monitor arm" upsell email
- Buyer of office chair (who hasn't bought desk) gets standing desk review video
- Desk buyer gets third-party review video to lower buyer's remorse
- Staff "thank you for reviews" video (4.7/5 stars — law of specificity) used for review requests or selling leads on customer happiness

**Key insight:** The video sold a $3,000 chair via email with subject line "zero gravity relaxation" — the video was the selling mechanism, delivered after trust was established through prior purchases.

## "Sent From iPhone" Engagement Bait Technique

When you need an extremely high response rate from an email to generate a ton of leads for the sales team or to juice your email stats for ESP reputation.

### What It Is
A short, sweet email that looks like you typed it on your iPhone and sent it straight to the person. Informal, brief, personal.

### Results
When sent to 400,000+ people who hadn't bought a $997 product, it generated THOUSANDS of replies. So many that multiple departments outside of marketing and sales — customer support, accounting team, even real estate guys — had to log into the inbox to batch-send responses to sales reps. All hands on deck.

### Template Format
```
hey [name],

[1-2 sentence personal-sounding message about the offer/opportunity]

[simple question or soft CTA]

Sent from my iPhone
```

### When to Use
- Flooding the sales team with leads
- Juicing email engagement metrics
- Re-engaging a stale list
- Promoting a specific limited offer

### Over 8 years of use with equally great results across multiple businesses.

---

Receiving an email with a photo of the founder holding a piece of paper with YOUR name on it creates an immediate wow effect.

# PART 2: EMAIL SEQUENCES

## Sequence 1: Pre-Call Nurture (The Money Maker)

**Purpose:** Maximize show rate and pre-frame leads so they arrive ready to buy
**Length:** 6-12 emails over 72 hours (2-4 per day)
**Goal:** Turn salespeople into "cashiers" — leads arrive pre-sold

### The 4 Content Pillars (From Hammer Them Strategy)

Every email maps to one of these pillars:

| Pillar | Purpose | Subject Line Style |
|--------|---------|-------------------|
| **Questions** | Answer what they fundamentally need to know | "Here's how [process] works..." |
| **2nd-Layer Questions** | Address follow-up questions | "But what if [concern]?" |
| **Objections** | Proactively handle resistance | "The #1 reason people hesitate..." |
| **Expectations** | Set realistic timelines and effort | "What your first 30 days look like" |

### Pre-Call Email Sequence Template

**Email 1: Booking Confirmation (Immediate)**
- Pillar: Expectations
- Subject: "You're confirmed — here's what happens next"
- Content: Confirm date/time, explain what the call covers, set expectations for call length, what to prepare, who they'll speak with
- CTA: "Add to your calendar" + link

**Email 2: The Story (Day 1, Morning)**
- Pillar: Questions
- Subject: "[Founder name]'s story — why we built [company]"
- Content: Founder/company origin story, the problem they noticed, why they're uniquely positioned to solve it, results achieved
- No hard CTA — pure trust building

**Email 3: Case Study (Day 1, Afternoon)**
- Pillar: Questions
- Subject: "How [client name] went from [before] to [after]"
- Content: Specific client case study matching the avatar, include numbers and timeline, show the transformation
- Soft CTA: "We'll discuss how we can do the same for you on our call"

**Email 4: Objection Handler #1 (Day 2, Morning)**
- Pillar: Objections
- Subject: "The #1 concern people have before our call"
- Content: Address the biggest objection head-on (usually price or "will this work for me"), reframe with evidence
- Soft CTA: "Bring any questions to our call — we'll cover everything"

**Email 5: The Process (Day 2, Afternoon)**
- Pillar: Expectations
- Subject: "Here's exactly what working with us looks like"
- Content: Step-by-step walkthrough of what happens after they sign up, timeline for results, what they'll need to do vs. what you handle
- CTA: "See you on [date] at [time]"

**Email 6: Social Proof Stack (Day 2, Evening)**
- Pillar: 2nd-Layer Questions
- Subject: "What [3 client names] have in common"
- Content: 3-5 brief testimonials with specific results, variety of industries/situations to show breadth
- Soft CTA: "Ready to be next? See you tomorrow."

**Email 7: Objection Handler #2 (Day 3, Morning)**
- Pillar: Objections
- Subject: "If you've tried [alternative] before and it didn't work..."
- Content: Address the "I've been burned before" objection, explain what makes this different (unique mechanism)
- CTA: "Our call is today at [time] — looking forward to it"

**Email 8: Day-Of Reminder (Day 3, 2 Hours Before)**
- Pillar: Expectations
- Subject: "Quick reminder — we're on in 2 hours"
- Content: Brief, friendly reminder. Reiterate value of the call. Link to join.
- CTA: "Click here to join at [time]"

**Email 9: 15-Minute Reminder (Day 3, 15 Min Before)**
- Pillar: Expectations
- Subject: "Starting in 15 minutes"
- Content: One line + join link
- CTA: "Join here"

### Optional Additional Emails (For 12-Email Version)

**Email 10:** Behind-the-scenes (team, office, process)
**Email 11:** FAQ format (5 most common questions)
**Email 12:** "What to expect on the call" (detailed agenda)

---

## Sequence 2: Post-Call Follow-Up (No Close)

**Purpose:** Re-engage leads who attended but didn't close
**Length:** 4-8 emails over 7-14 days
**Trigger:** Call completed, not closed

### Post-Call Email Sequence Template

**Email 1: Thank You + Recap (Same Day)**
- Subject: "Great speaking with you today, [name]"
- Content: Personalized recap of what was discussed, restate the specific plan/proposal, address any concerns raised on the call
- CTA: "Reply to this email if you have any questions"

**Email 2: The Urgency (Day 2)**
- Subject: "Quick question about [their goal]"
- Content: Reference something specific from the call, introduce soft urgency (limited spots, price increasing, timeline)
- CTA: "Ready to get started? [Link to payment/sign-up]"

**Email 3: Testimonial Match (Day 4)**
- Subject: "Someone in a similar situation as you..."
- Content: Case study that matches their specific situation/objection from the call
- CTA: "If [client name] can do it, so can you. [Link]"

**Email 4: The Cost of Waiting (Day 7)**
- Subject: "What another month of [pain point] is costing you"
- Content: Quantify the cost of inaction, contrast with the investment, show the ROI math
- CTA: "Let's not let another month go by. [Link]"

**Email 5: Objection Buster (Day 10)**
- Subject: "I wanted to address something"
- Content: Address their specific objection (ideally based on call notes), provide new evidence or angle
- CTA: "Want to hop on a quick follow-up? [Booking link]"

**Email 6: Final Offer (Day 14)**
- Subject: "Last chance — [specific incentive]"
- Content: Time-limited incentive (bonus, discount, payment plan), clear deadline
- CTA: "This expires [date]. [Link]"

---

## Sequence 3: No-Show Follow-Up

**Purpose:** Re-book leads who didn't show up
**Length:** 3-5 emails over 5 days

**Email 1:** "We missed you!" (same day) — Friendly, offer to rebook, no guilt
**Email 2:** Value reminder (day 2) — Reiterate what they would have learned, include a mini-insight
**Email 3:** Easy rebook (day 3) — One-click rebooking link, remove friction
**Email 4:** Social proof (day 5) — "While you decide, here's what [client] achieved..."
**Email 5:** Last touch (day 7) — "Still interested? No pressure — just reply 'yes' and I'll send options"

# PART 3: OPT-IN EMAIL SEQUENCE (AI Copywriting SOP)

## 5-Email Opt-In Sequence — Complete AI Prompt

For VSL funnels that have an opt-in OR for lead magnet funnels that require inputting an email. These prospects demonstrated interest by opting in and potentially watching some or all of your VSL, yet something prevented them from taking immediate action.

### Verbatim Prompt

```
You have been provided with comprehensive documentation about an offer including Benefits, Value Proposition, Pain Points, Questions, Concerns, Sales Argument, and the core VSL script. Your task is to create a strategic five-email sequence for prospects who opted into the VSL funnel but did not immediately book a call. This sequence must work as an integrated system that progressively overcomes resistance while building desire and urgency to schedule a consultation.

Understanding the Psychological Context
These prospects have demonstrated interest by opting in and potentially watching some or all of your VSL, yet something prevented them from taking immediate action. They exist in a specific psychological state characterized by simultaneous interest and hesitation. Your email sequence must diagnose and address the specific barriers preventing action while maintaining the momentum created by the initial engagement. Each email serves as both a continuation of the VSL conversation and a standalone persuasion piece that moves them closer to booking a call.

Email Sequence Architecture and Timing
The sequence should deploy over five days, with strategic spacing that balances persistence with respect. The psychological journey moves from reengagement and curiosity renewal through education and trust building to urgency and final conversion. Each email must provide standalone value while contributing to the larger narrative arc that makes booking a call feel increasingly necessary and decreasingly risky.

Email One: The Reengagement Bridge (Send immediately after opt-in)
This email serves as the critical bridge between their initial interest and continued engagement. The subject line should acknowledge their interest while creating a new curiosity loop that compels opening. The opening should immediately reward their decision to opt in by delivering unexpected value or insight not covered in the VSL. This positions you as someone who overdelivers while subtly suggesting how much more value awaits in a personal consultation.

The body should reframe their hesitation as intelligent caution while demonstrating why that caution, while admirable, may be costing them more than they realize. Include a soft call to action that makes booking a call feel like a natural next step rather than a sales pressure. The psychological goal is to maintain momentum while beginning to address the primary hesitation that prevented immediate booking.

Provide specific guidance on using personal, conversational language that feels like a continuation of a discussion rather than the beginning of a sales sequence. Include notes on optimal subject line patterns that achieve high open rates while maintaining trust and relevance.

Email Two: The Paradigm Expansion
This email's purpose is to expand their understanding of the problem and solution beyond what the VSL covered, demonstrating ongoing thought leadership while creating new reasons to engage personally. The subject line should promise a specific insight or revelation that builds on but doesn't repeat the VSL content.

Open with a story, case study, hypothetical situation, or example scenario, specifically chosen to address a common but unspoken concern your prospects harbor. This narrative should demonstrate transformation in someone who initially shared their exact hesitation, subtly showing that their resistance is both normal and surmountable. The narrative should reveal additional layers of the problem they face, making inaction feel increasingly costly while positioning a consultation as the logical path to clarity. Do not frame this narrative as something that has actually happened, because we do not want to lie about fake stories.

Include a teaching section that provides genuine tactical value they can implement immediately, demonstrating your expertise while creating a small win that increases trust. This tactical content should be valuable enough to justify the email but limited enough to highlight the need for personalized guidance. Close with a stronger call to action that references their specific situation and the cost of continued delay.

Email Three: The Authority Demonstration
This email establishes undeniable authority and social proof while addressing the skepticism that often prevents booking calls with unknown providers. The subject line should intrigue without appearing boastful, perhaps highlighting an unexpected result or counterintuitive insight.

Begin by acknowledging the proliferation of claimed experts in your field and the difficulty of distinguishing genuine expertise from marketing hype. Then systematically demonstrate your unique qualifications through specific, verifiable achievements that directly relate to the prospect's desired outcomes. This should go beyond simple testimonials to include concrete methodologies, frameworks, or insights that only deep expertise could produce.

Present a detailed case study that mirrors your prospect's situation closely enough to feel relevant but includes enough specific details to feel authentic rather than fabricated. This case study should address not just the ultimate success but the journey, including obstacles overcome and lessons learned that only experience could provide. The goal is to make prospects feel they are missing crucial insights available only through direct consultation.

Include a risk reversal element that specifically addresses the fear of wasting time on an unproductive call. This might take the form of a valuable guarantee about the call itself, such as a specific breakthrough or insight they will definitely receive regardless of whether they proceed further.

If you need additional information in order to fully complete this email, please add a note in your output. This may be necessary since we don't want to make up fake data or stories.

Email Four: The Urgency Catalyst
This email creates legitimate urgency through the revelation of time-sensitive factors they may not have considered. The subject line should convey movement and time sensitivity without resorting to false scarcity tactics that could erode trust.

Open by introducing a temporal element to their problem that makes delay genuinely costly. This could be market changes, competitive dynamics, seasonal factors, or the compound cost of prolonged inaction. The key is to help them realize that their problem is not static but dynamically worsening while they hesitate, making each day of delay more expensive than the last.

Present specific examples of prospects who waited too long and the concrete consequences they faced, balanced with examples of those who acted decisively and the advantages they captured. This creates a clear dichotomy between action and inaction that goes beyond simple fear-based marketing to genuine education about opportunity costs.

Introduce any legitimate scarcity elements such as calendar availability, cohort timing, or resource limitations that make immediate action genuinely advantageous. The call to action should emphasize the specific window of opportunity they are in and what closing that window means for their goals.

Email Five: The Final Invitation
This email serves as the final compelling invitation that combines all previous psychological triggers into an irresistible case for action. The subject line should create a sense of finality and opportunity simultaneously, making it clear this is the last direct invitation they will receive.

Open with a direct but warm acknowledgment that this is your final reach out in this sequence, positioning it as respect for their time rather than abandonment of interest. Summarize the complete journey from problem through solution to transformation in a condensed, powerful narrative that reminds them why they were interested initially and what remains available to them.

Address the meta-conversation about decision-making itself, helping them recognize if they are falling into analysis paralysis or fear-based procrastination that keeps them stuck regardless of the specific opportunity. This psychological pattern interrupt can help them see their hesitation as a symptom of the very problem your solution addresses.

Present a final, enhanced call to action that might include a limited-time bonus, priority scheduling, or special consultation offer available only to those who have engaged with the full sequence. This rewards their attention while creating a genuine advantage to acting now rather than returning later through a different path.

Close with a postscript that provides one final psychological trigger, perhaps a profound question that reframes their situation or a final success story that mirrors their exact circumstances. The postscript should feel like a personal note rather than marketing copy, maintaining human connection even as you respect their decision-making autonomy.

Technical Specifications for Each Email
Each email should include multiple subject line variations for testing, with each variation targeting a different psychological trigger while maintaining authenticity. Provide specific guidance on optimal email length for each message, generally ranging from 300-600 words for earlier emails to potentially 600-1200 words for the more substantive middle emails, while keeping the final email concise and action-focused.

Include preview text optimization that works in conjunction with the subject line to maximize open rates without resorting to deceptive practices. Specify the optimal call-to-action placement and frequency for each email, ensuring every message provides a clear path to booking while not overwhelming with excessive repetition.

Sequence Integration Requirements
The entire sequence must feel like a cohesive conversation rather than five separate sales attempts. Include specific callback references that create continuity between emails while allowing each to stand alone for those who might miss one or engage out of sequence. Provide guidance on how to reference the VSL content without requiring they have watched it completely, making the emails valuable regardless of their level of prior engagement.

Create a sophistication progression that assumes increasing knowledge and awareness with each email, allowing later messages to make bolder claims and more direct appeals based on the foundation built by earlier ones. Include specific phrases and transitions that maintain this progression while preventing redundancy or repetition that could trigger unsubscribes.

Output Format Requirements
For each email, provide the complete copy including subject lines, preview text, body copy, and call-to-action sections. Include strategic notes explaining the psychological mechanism each element employs and why specific choices were made. Provide confidence scores for each email's likely effectiveness and specific split-testing recommendations for continuous optimization.

The final sequence should feel like a valuable educational journey that happens to conclude with a consultation opportunity, rather than a series of increasingly desperate sales pitches. Each prospect should finish the sequence either having booked a call or possessing genuinely valuable insights that improve their situation regardless, preserving goodwill and future opportunity even among non-converters.

Do not proceed until you have fully internalized the offer documentation to understand both what drives interest and what creates hesitation in your specific prospect base. The sequence must address both aspects with sophistication and respect.
```

# PART 4: BROADCAST EMAIL STRATEGIES

## Overview

Broadcast emails are one-off emails sent to the list (not automated sequences). You NEED sourced materials for these to work — provide the LLM a base of what you talk about.

### Required Source Materials (provide to AI)
- Other emails sent before
- Consulting calls / coaching calls transcripts
- Sales calls where advice was given
- YouTube video transcripts
- LinkedIn posts / Twitter posts
- Webinar transcripts
- Courses/products already made (get the transcripts)
- eBooks / any form of written content ever made

## Strategy 1: Trust then Strike

### Weekly Cadence
| Day | Type | CTA Level |
|-----|------|-----------|
| Monday | Value Email | Light or no CTA |
| Tuesday | Value Email | Light or no CTA |
| Wednesday | **Sales Email** | **Full pitch for the offer** |
| Thursday | Value Email | Light or no CTA |
| Friday | Value Email | Light or no CTA |

### Verbatim AI Prompt — Trust then Strike

```
You have been provided with various text transcripts from the client's existing content library including past emails, consulting/coaching calls, sales conversations, video transcripts, social media posts, webinars, courses, and written materials. Your task is to analyze this source material deeply to understand their expertise, teaching style, and value delivery patterns, then generate authentic broadcast emails that feel like natural extensions of their existing body of work.

Content Analysis Framework
Before generating any emails, conduct a thorough analysis of the provided materials to extract:

Voice Fingerprint: Identify the specific linguistic patterns, phrases, and expressions that make their communication distinctive. Note their typical sentence structure, whether they use questions to engage readers, their level of formality, their use of personal anecdotes versus pure teaching, and any signature phrases or concepts they regularly return to. Pay particular attention to how they transition between ideas and how they naturally introduce their expertise without appearing boastful.

Value Architecture: Map the specific types of value they provide across different contexts. Do they primarily teach through frameworks, stories, contrarian insights, or step-by-step tactics? Identify their core teachings and the various angles from which they approach their central expertise. Note which concepts they consider fundamental versus advanced, and how they scaffold complexity for their audience.

Topic Ecosystem: Create a comprehensive inventory of subjects they cover, but more importantly, understand the connections between these topics. How do they link different ideas? What examples do they repeatedly use? What problems do they consistently address? What transformations do they promise? Understanding their topic ecosystem allows you to generate emails that feel coherent with their broader message while avoiding redundancy.

Natural CTA Patterns: Analyze how they naturally transition from value delivery to offers. Do they use soft suggestions, direct invitations, assumption closes, or value-stacking approaches? How do they mention their products or services without breaking the flow of value delivery? What specific language do they use when inviting action?

Email Generation Strategy by Day

Monday Value Email - The Week Starter
This email should feel like beginning a conversation that will naturally evolve throughout the week. Pull from their consulting or coaching calls where they're introducing new concepts or reframing familiar problems. The tone should be energizing but not overwhelming, setting an intellectual or emotional theme that makes the reader want to stay engaged all week.
Structure this as pure value with either no CTA or an extremely soft one like "Something to think about this week" or "Try this and let me know how it goes." The psychological goal is to provide immediate Monday morning value that makes opening future emails feel rewarding rather than salesy.
Draw specifically from moments in their content where they're teaching foundational concepts or sharing breakthrough insights. If they have a signature framework or methodology, Monday is ideal for introducing one aspect of it without feeling like you're holding back to force a sale.

Tuesday Value Email - The Deep Dive
Building on Monday's theme if possible, this email should provide tactical depth. Pull from transcripts where they're actually walking someone through implementation or providing specific examples. This email can be slightly longer as readers have already been primed by Monday's content.
The Tuesday email should feel like they're sitting beside the reader, actually helping them solve a problem. Include specific examples from their content library, but adapt them slightly so they feel fresh rather than recycled. If Monday introduced a concept, Tuesday shows how it actually works in practice.
Any CTA here should feel like a natural extension of the value, such as "If you want to go even deeper on this..." or "I cover this in more detail in [resource]..." without pressure or urgency.

Wednesday Sales Email - The Natural Pitch
This is your only direct sales message of the week, but it shouldn't feel jarring. Build it from sales call transcripts where they're actually enrolling clients, but adapt the language for one-to-many communication. The email should acknowledge the value shared earlier in the week and position the offer as the logical next step for those ready to go further.
Start with a brief value reminder or insight to maintain consistency, then transition naturally into the problem their offer solves. Use their actual language from sales conversations where they're explaining why someone needs their solution. Include the specific benefits and outcomes they promise in their sales calls, maintaining their authentic voice rather than switching to generic sales copy.
The CTA should be clear and direct with a specific action: "Book your call here," "Get instant access," or whatever action they typically request. Include any authentic urgency or scarcity from their actual offer, but don't manufacture false pressure if they don't normally use it.

Thursday Value Email - The Recovery
After Wednesday's pitch, Thursday returns to pure value but can cleverly relate to the offer without selling it. For instance, if Wednesday pitched a course on X, Thursday might share a powerful insight about X that stands alone as valuable content. This maintains topical coherence while respecting those who didn't purchase.
Pull from their teaching content where they're giving away genuinely useful information without holding back. This email rebuilds pure goodwill and demonstrates abundance mindset. It should feel like they're saying, "Whether you bought or not, I'm still here to help."
The CTA should be minimal, perhaps just encouraging engagement: "Reply and tell me your biggest challenge with this" or "Forward this to someone who needs to hear it."

Friday Value Email - The Gift
End the week with something special—their best story, their most counterintuitive insight, or their most actionable framework. Pull from their absolute best content moments, the ones that would make someone forward the email or save it for reference.
Friday's email should feel like a gift that creates anticipation for next week. It might include a useful resource, a powerful reframe, or an inspiring story from their content library. The tone should be slightly more casual and personal, acknowledging the week's end while providing value that lingers into the weekend.
Any CTA should be relationship-focused rather than transaction-focused: "Have a great weekend," "Let me know if you try this," or at most, "If you want more content like this, here's where to find it."

Technical Writing Specifications
Length: Each email should typically run 300-600 words, though this can vary based on their natural style discovered in the source material. Sales emails may be longer (up to 1000 words) if that matches their selling style.
Format: Pure text with line breaks for readability. No bold, italics, bullets, or special formatting. Use capital letters sparingly for emphasis if that matches their style. Include strategic line breaks to create visual breathing room, with single sentences sometimes standing alone for impact.
Subject Lines: Generate three variations for each email:
- Curiosity-driven (opens a loop that the email closes)
- Benefit-driven (promises specific value)
- Personal/casual (feels like a note from a friend)
Analyze their previous subject lines if available and match their style—do they use sentence case or title case? Do they use punctuation? How long are they typically?
Voice Consistency: Every email must sound like it could only have come from this person. Use their specific phrases, their typical examples, their preferred analogies. If they always talk about business through sports metaphors, use sports metaphors. If they never curse, don't curse. If they frequently use rhetorical questions, include them.

Value Extraction Guidelines
When pulling from source materials, adapt rather than copy. If a coaching call includes a great explanation, transform it from dialogue to narrative. If a social media post contains a powerful insight, expand it into email length with additional context and examples. If a course module teaches a framework, extract one component for a single email rather than trying to compress everything.
Always prioritize insights that are immediately actionable or mentally transformative. The reader should finish each email feeling either "I can do this right now" or "I've never thought about it this way before."

Output Requirements
For each email, provide:
- The day of the week and email type
- Three subject line options
- The complete email text with proper line breaks
- A brief note explaining which source materials inspired this email and how you adapted them
- The specific CTA used and why it's appropriate for this day's strategy
- A confidence score (1-10) that this email authentically represents their voice and value
Generate emails that feel like natural extensions of their existing content library while providing fresh value. The weekly sequence should feel cohesive without being repetitive, valuable without being overwhelming, and authentic without being predictable. The ultimate test: Could someone familiar with their work believe they personally wrote these emails?
Do not proceed until you have thoroughly analyzed all provided transcripts to understand their unique voice, teaching style, and value delivery patterns. The emails must feel genuinely authored by them, not generically professional.
```

## Strategy 2: Gentle Drip

### Weekly Cadence
| Day | Type | CTA Level |
|-----|------|-----------|
| Monday | Value Email | Light/Medium Pitch |
| Tuesday | Value Email | Light or no CTA |
| Wednesday | Value Email | Light/Medium Pitch |
| Thursday | Value Email | Light or no CTA |
| Friday | Value Email | Light or no CTA |

### Key Differences from Strategy 1
- NO dedicated sales email — every email delivers value with integrated soft selling
- Value-to-pitch ratio: approximately 80:20 or 70:30
- 2-3 natural mentions of the offer per email (one subtle woven into teaching, one slightly more direct with context, one clear but soft CTA at end)
- Embed links naturally within sentences rather than standalone "Click here" CTAs

### Integration Techniques for Natural Selling

**The Mention Weave:** Rather than dedicated pitch sections, weave mentions throughout. Reference your program as an example, cite client results as evidence, mention resources as additional learning.

**The Soft Assumption:** Write as if some readers are already considering your offer. "For those of you who have been thinking about [program]..." Creates inevitability without pressure.

**The Value Stack:** Each email provides standalone value while subtly highlighting depth available in paid offer. Teach one piece thoroughly while naturally mentioning the broader system.

**The Permission Pattern:** Give readers permission not to buy while making the option attractive: "You can absolutely do this on your own. Here's how... But if you want to go faster with support, I'm here."

### Day-by-Day Architecture

**Monday — The Possibility Opener:** Open mental space for transformation. Light mention: "This is exactly what I work on with clients in [program]" or "I go deeper into this in [resource], but here's what you need to know right now..."

**Tuesday — The Method Reveal:** Tactical value demonstrating expertise. Medium mention: "This is step 2 of the framework I teach in [program]. While the full system has 7 steps, this one alone can make a significant difference..."

**Wednesday — The Case Study Teacher:** Teaches through success story example. Natural mention: "When they joined [program], they were struggling with X. Here's what we discovered together..."

**Thursday — The Obstacle Dissolver:** Addresses objections from sales calls/FAQ content. Mention: "Of course, if you want to accelerate this process, that's exactly why I created [program]..."

**Friday — The Vision Caster:** Inspires and motivates. Mention: "If you're ready to make this your reality, I'd love to help. Here's what that could look like..."

### Technical Specs
- Length: 400-700 words per email
- Mention frequency: 2-3 natural mentions per email
- Transition phrases: "This is exactly why...", "Speaking of which...", "This reminds me of what we do in...", "If you want to take this further...", "For those ready to implement this fully..."

## Strategy 3: Enduring Pitch

### Weekly Cadence
| Day | Type | CTA Level |
|-----|------|-----------|
| Monday | Value Email | Light/Medium (seed planting) |
| Tuesday | Value Email | Medium (tension building + anticipation) |
| Wednesday | **Sales Email** | **Full pitch for the offer** |
| Thursday | Value Email | Light (graceful recovery) |
| Friday | Value Email | Light (generous close) |

### Key Differences from Strategy 1
- Monday and Tuesday actively BUILD TOWARD Wednesday's pitch (crescendo strategy)
- Build-release-recover rhythm
- Monday plants seed, Tuesday builds tension and creates anticipation ("Tomorrow I'm going to share something special...")
- Wednesday is longer (800-1200 words) — complete sales conversation
- Thursday acknowledges both buyers AND non-buyers gracefully

### Day-by-Day Architecture

**Monday — The Foundation Setter:** Introduce week's theme. Mention: "I've been working with several clients on exactly this challenge..." Plant a seed without requiring decision.

**Tuesday — The Tension Builder:** Deepen the problem. Build anticipation: "Tomorrow I'm going to share something special for those ready to take real action on this, but for now, here's what you can do today..." 2-3 mentions that build subtle momentum.

**Wednesday — The Full Enrollment Conversation:** Open by acknowledging the week's journey. Problem amplification using authentic sales call language. Solution presentation using exact framework from sales conversations. Social proof section (2-3 powerful stories). Offer structure clearly presented. Risk reversal. Multiple clear CTAs throughout.

**Thursday — The Graceful Recovery:** Open with fresh value, NOT a reference to yesterday's pitch. "Whether you're implementing this on your own or joining us in [program], here's something that will help..." Serve both buyers and non-buyers.

**Friday — The Generous Close:** Peak value. "This is the kind of thing we dive deep into in [program], but I wanted to share it with everyone because it's too important to gatekeep..." P.S.: "If you've been thinking about [program], we still have a few spots open. But either way, try this technique..."

### Technical Specs
- Value emails: 400-700 words, 85:15 or 80:20 value-to-pitch, 1-3 offer mentions, light-medium CTA
- Sales email: 800-1200 words, 30:70 or 20:80 value-to-pitch, 3-5 CTAs, direct and action-oriented

### When to Use Which Strategy
Oscillate between all strategies based on audience reaction:

- If calls/sales slow down (audience being tapped out), switch to building more trust — likely back to Trust then Strike
- Monitor engagement metrics continuously and adapt
